title: Testing, Debugging, and Deployment
summary: Prove your Apex works, find out fast when it doesn't, and move it safely to production.

lessons.title: Tests and the 75% Rule
lessons.objective: Write and execute tests for triggers, controllers, classes, and flows using various sources of test data.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **test class** is Apex that checks your other Apex. It runs your code with known data. Then it checks the result. Salesforce also uses tests as a gate. Without enough tests, your code can't reach production.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A driving test. The examiner watches you drive real roads and checks each move. Where it stops: an examiner can't pass you just for driving. Coverage can. It only proves lines ran, so you add **asserts** to prove the results are right.

cards.title: A tiny test class
cards.body: `@IsTest` marks the class and each **test method**. A test method is `static`, takes no arguments and returns nothing. The **assert** checks the answer.

cards.title: The deploy gate
items: At least **75%** of your Apex is covered by tests
All of those tests pass
Every **trigger** has some coverage
All classes and triggers **compile**

cards.title: How coverage is counted
cards.body: **Code coverage** = covered lines ÷ (covered + uncovered lines). Only executable lines count. Test classes and `System.debug` lines are left out. See your numbers on the **Tests tab** of the Developer Console.

cards.title: Where tests live
cards.body: Since API 28.0, test methods must sit in a class marked `@IsTest`. The class can be `private`; the framework still finds it. Test classes don't count against the org's code size limit.
"75% for every class" is the classic wrong answer. The default gate is 75% **overall**. One class at 40% can still ship if the total is 75%. But one trigger at 0% blocks the deploy.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: "**75, all pass, every trigger.**" Coverage gets you in the door. Asserts prove the code is right.

terms.say: A class that only holds test code. It is marked with `@IsTest` and never runs for real users.
A check inside a test. It says what the answer should be. If the real answer is different, the test fails.
A label you put on a test class and its test methods. It tells Salesforce this code is only for testing.
One check inside a test class. It is static, takes no inputs and gives nothing back.
Apex that runs by itself when records are saved. Every trigger needs at least some test coverage before it can go to production.
Turn your code into something Salesforce can run. Code with mistakes doesn't compile, so it can't be deployed.
How much of your code the tests actually ran, as a percent. Lines that ran count as covered.
A line that writes a note into the debug log. It doesn't count as a covered or uncovered line.
A tab at the bottom of the Developer Console. It shows test results and how much of each class the tests covered.
The most Apex an org can hold. Classes marked `@IsTest` don't use up any of it.

lessons.title: Test Data You Control
lessons.objective: Write and execute tests for triggers, controllers, classes, and flows using various sources of test data.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A test needs records to work on. Real org records change all the time, so tests shouldn't depend on them. By default a test sees an **empty org** and makes its own data. When it ends, everything it made is **rolled back**. Nothing is ever saved.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A flight simulator. Pilots crash planes there and nothing real breaks. Every session starts from the same setup. Where it stops: a few setup things are always there, like `User`, `Profile` and `RecordType` records.

cards.title: Data isolation
cards.body: Since API **24.0**, tests can't see org data such as Accounts or custom setting records. They can still see setup and metadata objects, like `User`, `Profile`, `Organization` and `RecordType`. `@IsTest(SeeAllData=true)` opens all data, but it isn't best practice.

cards.title: A test data factory
cards.body: A **test data factory** is one shared `@IsTest` class that builds records. Only test code can call it, and it doesn't use up the code size limit.

cards.title: Set up once
cards.body: `@TestSetup` runs once, before any test method. Each test method then sees the **original** records. One method's changes roll back before the next. Only one per class.

cards.title: Data from a CSV
cards.body: `Test.loadData` reads a CSV **static resource** and inserts each row. The first line holds the field names. It returns the new records.

`SeeAllData=true` lets a test read org data, but its inserts and updates are **still rolled back**. Also, a class with `SeeAllData=true` can't use `@TestSetup`, and a method can't switch it back off with `SeeAllData=false`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: "**Pack your own lunch.**" A test eats only what it brings: a factory, `@TestSetup` or a CSV with `Test.loadData`.

terms.say: In a test, the org looks empty. The test can't see the real records, so it makes the ones it needs.
Undone. When a test ends, every record it made or changed goes back to how it was. Nothing is saved.
A setting that lets a test see the org's real records. Avoid it, because those records change and can break the test.
A small store of settings data. Its records are org data, so a test can't see them unless it creates them.
One shared helper class that builds test records. Every test asks it for data, so a change is made in one place.
A method that makes test records once for the whole class. Each test method then starts from that same fresh copy.
The records exactly as `@TestSetup` made them. Changes from an earlier test method are gone.
Reads a CSV file stored in Salesforce and inserts each row as a record. You get test data without writing it in code.
A file you upload to Salesforce, like a CSV or an image. Code can read it later.
Records that describe the org itself, like users and profiles. Tests can always see these.

lessons.title: startTest, stopTest and Async
lessons.objective: Write and execute tests for triggers, controllers, classes, and flows using various sources of test data.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Tests have two jobs: prepare, then act. `Test.startTest()` and `Test.stopTest()` wrap the act part. The code between them gets its own fresh **governor limits**. And any **async** work started inside finishes when `stopTest` runs.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A race with a starting gun and a finish line. Warm-up laps before the gun don't count. At the finish line, every runner still on the track is made to finish. Where it stops: you get only one race per test method.

cards.title: The rules
items: Each one is called **once** per test method
Code between them gets a **new set of limits**
After `stopTest`, the original limits come back
Async calls made after `startTest` run **synchronously** at `stopTest`

cards.title: Testing a Queueable
cards.body: Data is made before `startTest`. The job runs at `stopTest`, so the assert after it sees the result.

cards.title: Batch Apex in tests
cards.body: A test can run only **one** `execute` call of a batch job. Keep test records within one batch scope. If `executeBatch` sits outside the block, the job runs at the **end** of the test method, after your asserts.

cards.title: Checking limits
cards.code:
Integer used = Limits.getQueries();
Integer max = Limits.getLimitQueries();
cards.body: The `Limits` class tells you what's used so far and the maximum for this context.
Asserting **before** `stopTest` is the classic bug. Async work hasn't run yet, so the record still looks old. Assert after `stopTest`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: "**Set up, start, act, stop, assert.**" Five steps, in that order, every time.

terms.say: Marks where the real test begins. Code after it gets a fresh set of limits.
Marks where the test ends. Any async work started after `startTest` runs right here.
Caps on how much one transaction can do, like 100 SOQL queries. They keep one org from hogging shared servers.
Work that runs later, not right now. Future methods, Queueable jobs and batch jobs are async.
Inside the start-stop block, the counters start again from zero. Setup work before it doesn't eat into them.
Right now, in order, while you wait. In a test, async jobs run this way at `stopTest`.
The batch method that handles one chunk of records. A test can run it only once.
The call that starts a batch job. In a test, put it between `startTest` and `stopTest`.
A class that reports how much of each limit you have used and what the maximum is.
How many records go into one `execute` call. The default is 200.

lessons.title: Testing Triggers, Controllers, Flows
lessons.objective: Write and execute tests for triggers, controllers, classes, and flows using various sources of test data.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: You can't call a trigger or a record-triggered flow from a test. You make them run the way users do: by saving records. Controllers are plain classes, so tests create them and call their methods. Then you check the results.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Testing a doorbell. You don't poke the wires. You press the button and listen for the ring. Where it stops: a Visualforce controller is more like a remote control. You can call its methods directly.

cards.title: A bulk trigger test
cards.body: The `insert` fires the **trigger**. Testing many records proves the trigger is **bulk-safe**. Best practice: use at least 20 records.

cards.title: Test the bad path too
cards.body: A **negative test** checks that bad data fails. Put the DML in `try`. Call `Assert.fail()` right after it, then check the error in `catch`. Without `Assert.fail()`, the test passes even if nothing failed.

cards.title: A controller extension
cards.body: `Test.setCurrentPage` sets the page and its URL parameters. The **extension** gets a **standard controller** built around a test record.

cards.title: Flows and LWC Apex
cards.body: A **record-triggered flow** runs when the test saves records, so assert its results. Admins can also build **flow tests** in Flow Builder. Apex can start an autolaunched flow with `Flow.Interview`. An `@AuraEnabled` method is tested by calling it directly.

cards.title: Run as another user
cards.body: `System.runAs(user)` runs a block as that user. Their **record sharing** applies. Their object and field permissions count only where the code checks them, like user mode. It works only in tests. It also lets one test create a `User` and an Account without a mixed DML error.
Inside `runAs`, a method from another class keeps **its own** sharing mode. A `without sharing` class still sees every record, whoever you run as.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: "**Save it to start it.**" Triggers and flows wake up on DML. Controllers get called. Every test ends with an assert.

terms.say: Apex that runs by itself when records are saved. A test makes it run by inserting or updating records.
Works just as well for 200 records as for 1. It doesn't hit limits when many records are saved at once.
A test that feeds in bad data and checks that it fails the right way.
Makes a test fail on purpose. Put it right after code that should have thrown an error.
Tells a test which Visualforce page is open, so a controller can read its URL parameters.
A class that adds extra features to a standard controller on a Visualforce page.
The ready-made controller Salesforce gives every object. A test builds one around a record.
A flow that runs by itself when a record is created, updated or deleted.
Checks you build in Flow Builder. They run a flow with a sample record and test the results.
Runs part of a test as a different user. Their record sharing applies. Their object and field permissions count only where the code checks them.

lessons.title: Debug Logs and Log Levels
lessons.objective: Describe how to approach debugging system issues and monitoring flows, performance, asynchronous, and batch jobs.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: When code misbehaves, you need to see what it did. A **debug log** records one transaction: database work, Apex, flows, validation rules and errors. A **trace flag** on a user turns logging on for a set time window.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A plane's black box. It records what happened so you can study it later. Where it stops: you choose how much it records. Turn it up only for what you're chasing, or the important part gets cut.

cards.title: Some log categories
items: **Apex Code**: Apex, including `System.debug` lines
**Database**: DML and SOQL
**Workflow**: workflow rules, **flows** and processes
**Validation**: validation rules
**Apex Profiling**: limit usage

cards.title: Log levels, quiet to loud
items: `NONE`, `ERROR`, `WARN`, `INFO`
`DEBUG`, `FINE`, `FINER`, `FINEST`
Each level includes everything quieter than it
`FINEST` on Apex Code logs every variable assignment

cards.title: Choosing a message level
cards.body: A plain `System.debug` logs at `DEBUG`. The second line logs at `ERROR`, so it shows even with a quiet **log level**.

cards.title: Log limits
items: Each log is at most **20 MB**; older lines get cut
System debug logs are kept **24 hours**
Monitoring logs are kept **7 days**
Over 1,000 MB in 15 minutes turns trace flags off

cards.body: A trace flag on a **class or trigger** doesn't create logs by itself. It only changes the levels while logging is already on, for example from a user trace flag.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: "**E, W, I, D, then three Fs**": Error, Warn, Info, Debug, Fine, Finer, Finest. Turn up only what you need.

terms.say: A record of what happened in one transaction. It shows queries, saves, errors and your own messages.
A setting that turns on logging for a user for a set time. On a class or trigger, it only changes how much gets logged.
The log category for Apex itself. Your `System.debug` messages appear under it.
The log category that covers workflow rules, flows and processes.
The log category that shows how much of each governor limit was used.
The loudest log level. It logs everything, even each variable change, so logs get big fast.
A line of Apex that writes your own message into the debug log.
How much detail a category records, from `NONE` (nothing) to `FINEST` (everything).
The biggest a single debug log can be. Past that, older lines are removed.
Click-built automation. Flow events show in the log under the Workflow category.

lessons.title: The Developer Console
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, know how and when to use the Salesforce Developer tools such as Salesforce DX, Salesforce CLI, and Developer Console.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The **Developer Console** is a code editor that opens in your browser, right inside your org. You can edit Apex, run tests, read logs and run queries. Nothing to install, so it's great for quick checks.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A toolbox on the workbench. Every tool is in reach for small jobs. Where it stops: big projects want a full workshop. That means VS Code with the Salesforce CLI and version control.

cards.title: What it does
items: **Execute Anonymous**: run a snippet of Apex now
**Logs tab** and **Log Inspector**: read debug logs
**Tests tab**: run tests, see code coverage
**Query Editor**: run SOQL and SOSL
**Checkpoints**: snapshots of memory at a line

cards.title: Execute Anonymous
cards.body: **Anonymous Apex** isn't saved as a class. It runs as the **current user**. Its changes are **committed** when it finishes without errors. If it fails, all its changes roll back. It can be a quick fix or a way to start a batch job.

cards.title: Query Editor
cards.body: Type SOQL or SOSL and run it. Tick **Use Tooling API** to query developer objects, like `ApexCodeCoverageAggregate` for coverage. The **Query Plan** button shows how costly a query is.

cards.title: Checkpoints and Log Inspector
cards.body: A **checkpoint** captures objects in memory at one line, without editing the code. **Log Inspector** shows a log in panels. **Execution Overview** shows where time and limits went.
Anonymous Apex is **not** a test. Records it inserts are real and stay in the org. Only test methods roll back their data.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: "**Run, read, query, peek.**" Run snippets and tests, read logs, query data, peek at memory with checkpoints.

terms.say: A code tool that opens in your browser inside your org. You can edit, test and debug there.
A window where you type some Apex and run it right away, without saving a class.
The Developer Console view that opens a debug log in easy-to-read panels.
The Developer Console tab where you type and run SOQL or SOSL queries.
Markers on a line of code. When that line runs, the console saves a snapshot of the objects in memory.
Apex you run once without saving it as a class. Its changes are real.
The person running the code. Anonymous Apex runs as you, with your permissions.
Saved for good in the database. Anonymous Apex commits its changes if it finishes without errors.
A checkbox in the Query Editor. It lets you query developer objects, like code coverage records.
The Log Inspector panel that shows where time went and how much of each limit was used.

lessons.title: Salesforce DX, CLI, Scratch Orgs
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, know how and when to use the Salesforce Developer tools such as Salesforce DX, Salesforce CLI, and Developer Console.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Salesforce DX** is a way of working where your project files, not an org, are the source of truth. You keep them in **version control** like Git. The **Salesforce CLI** (the `sf` command) moves them in and out of orgs.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A recipe book. The recipes (your project) are kept safe. Each **scratch org** is a fresh meal cooked from them, eaten, then cleared away. Where it stops: a meal goes bad in days. A scratch org lasts 30 days at most.

cards.title: Project files
items: `sfdx-project.json`: the project's main settings
`force-app/`: your metadata, in source format
`config/project-scratch-def.json`: the **scratch org definition file**

cards.title: Scratch orgs
cards.body: A **scratch org** is a short-lived, empty org built from source. You need a **Dev Hub** org to create one. It lasts **1 to 30 days**, 7 by default. Once expired, it **can't be restored**. **Source tracking** is on by default.

cards.title: The everyday loop
cards.code:
sf org login web --set-default-dev-hub --alias DevHub
sf org create scratch --definition-file config/project-scratch-def.json --alias dev --set-default
sf project deploy start
sf apex run test --code-coverage --result-format human
sf project retrieve start
cards.body: Log in to the Dev Hub, create a scratch org, **deploy** your source, run tests, then **retrieve** changes you made in the org.

cards.title: Handy CLI commands
cards.body: `sf apex run --file` runs anonymous Apex from a file. `sf apex tail log` shows debug logs live in your terminal. `sf org open` opens an org in the browser without typing a password.
A scratch org is **not** a copy of production. It starts empty: no custom objects, no data, no Apex. Need production's metadata and data? That's a **sandbox**.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: "**Hub, create, deploy, test, retrieve.**" And scratch orgs live 7 days unless you ask for up to 30.

terms.say: A way of building where your project files are the main copy. Orgs are just places you send them.
A tool like Git that saves every change to your files, so you can see history and undo mistakes.
A command-line tool, typed as `sf`, that talks to your orgs. It deploys, retrieves, runs tests and more.
A short-lived, empty org you build from your project files. You throw it away when you're done.
A small JSON file that says what a scratch org should look like: edition, features and settings.
The main org that creates and keeps track of your scratch orgs. Often it's your production org.
The CLI notes what changed in your files and in the org, so it can sync just those changes.
Send your project files into an org.
Pull changes made in an org back into your project files.
A copy of your production org's setup, and sometimes its data, for building and testing safely.

lessons.title: Sandboxes and Other Orgs
lessons.objective: Describe the environments, requirements, and process for deploying code and associated configurations.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: You can't write Apex in **production**, the org real users work in. You build and test somewhere safe first. A **sandbox** is a copy of production's setup. Some sandbox types also copy data.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Rehearsals before opening night. Early ones happen in a small room. The dress rehearsal is on the real stage, with every costume and prop. Where it stops: that big stage copy can only be rebuilt every 29 days.

cards.title: Sandbox cheat sheet
items: **Developer**: metadata only, 200 MB data, refresh every **1 day**
**Developer Pro**: metadata only, 1 GB data, refresh every **1 day**
**Partial Copy**: metadata + sample data, 5 GB, every **5 days**
**Full**: metadata + all data, same as production, every **29 days**

cards.title: Sandbox templates
cards.body: A **sandbox template** picks which objects' data gets copied. **Partial Copy** needs one. **Full** can use one if you want less than everything.

cards.title: Which one when?
items: Coding and unit tests: **Developer** or **Developer Pro**
QA and integration tests with real-looking data: **Partial Copy**
Performance tests, load tests and staging: **Full**

cards.title: Other places to build
cards.body: A **Developer Edition** org is a free, standalone org. A **scratch org** is built from source and short-lived. Neither one is a copy of your production org.
Developer and Developer Pro copy **no records**. Need data for tests there? Load it yourself. Need lots of real data? Pick Partial Copy or Full.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: Refresh days "**1, 1, 5, 29**": Developer, Developer Pro, Partial Copy, Full. Bigger sandbox, longer wait.

terms.say: The live org where real users do real work. You can't develop Apex directly in it.
A copy of your production org's setup for building and testing, kept apart from real users.
The smallest sandbox. It copies setup only, holds 200 MB of data and refreshes daily.
Like a Developer sandbox, but with 1 GB of data storage. It also copies setup only.
A sandbox with setup plus a sample of your data, picked by a template. It refreshes every 5 days.
A sandbox that copies all setup and all data. It refreshes only every 29 days.
A list of which objects' records get copied into a Partial Copy or Full sandbox.
Rebuild a sandbox as a new copy of production. Each type has a minimum wait between refreshes.
A free, separate Salesforce org for learning and building. It isn't tied to your production org.
A short-lived, empty org built from your project files with the Salesforce CLI.

lessons.title: Deploying and Watching Jobs
lessons.objective: Describe the environments, requirements, and process for deploying code and associated configurations.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Deploying** means moving code and settings from one org to another, usually sandbox to production. On the way in, production runs tests. Afterward, you watch async jobs and flows to catch problems early.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Moving house. You pack boxes (metadata), check nothing is broken (tests) and unpack in the new home. Where it stops: if one box fails the check, the whole move is cancelled. Nothing is half-delivered to production.

cards.title: Change sets
cards.body: A **change set** is built by clicking in Setup. You add components to an **outbound** change set in the source org. It arrives as an **inbound** change set. It works only between connected orgs, like a sandbox and its production org. Change sets can't delete components.

cards.title: Deploying with the CLI
cards.code:
sf project deploy start --manifest manifest/package.xml --test-level RunLocalTests
sf project deploy validate --manifest manifest/package.xml --test-level RunLocalTests
sf project deploy quick --job-id 0Af000000000001
cards.body: Deploy with a **package.xml** list. Or **validate** first, then **quick deploy** within 10 days without re-running tests.

cards.title: Test levels
items: `NoTestRun`: dev orgs and sandboxes only; their default
`RunSpecifiedTests`: only named tests; each deployed class and trigger needs 75%
`RunLocalTests`: all tests not from installed packages; production default with Apex
`RunAllTestsInOrg`: every test, packages too

cards.title: Watching an async job
cards.body: `executeBatch` and `System.enqueueJob` return a job Id. Query **AsyncApexJob** with it, or open **Apex Jobs** in Setup.

cards.title: Watching flows
cards.body: In a debug log, flow events appear under the **Workflow** category. Flow Builder's **Debug** button runs a flow and shows each step it took. Scheduled Apex shows on the **Scheduled Jobs** page.
`NoTestRun` is not allowed for production. Also, a quick deploy needs a validation that passed in the last **10 days**. Older? Validate again.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: "**Pack, check, ship, watch.**" Change set or CLI, tests on the way in, then Apex Jobs and logs on the way out.

terms.say: Moving code and settings from one org into another, like from a sandbox to production.
A bundle of changes you build by clicking in Setup and send to a connected org.
A change set you are sending out from this org.
A change set that arrived in this org, waiting to be checked and deployed.
A list file that names every component to deploy or retrieve.
A practice deploy. It runs the tests and checks everything, but saves nothing.
Deploys a passed validation without running the tests again. It must happen within 10 days.
A record for each async Apex job. It shows the job's status, progress and errors.
A Setup page that lists async Apex jobs and their status. You can stop a batch job there.
A Setup page that lists jobs set to run at certain times, like scheduled Apex.

flashcards.front: What must be true before Apex can deploy to production?
flashcards.back: At least 75% of Apex is covered by tests, all those tests pass, every trigger has some coverage, and everything compiles.

flashcards.front: How is code coverage calculated?
flashcards.back: Covered lines divided by covered plus uncovered lines. Only executable lines count. Test classes and `System.debug` lines are left out.

flashcards.front: Can a test method live in a normal Apex class?
flashcards.back: No. Since API 28.0, test methods must be in a class marked `@IsTest`. The class can be private.

flashcards.front: Does 100% coverage prove the code is right?
flashcards.back: No. Coverage only shows lines ran. Use `Assert` methods to check the results are correct.

flashcards.front: Can a test see the records already in the org?
flashcards.back: Not by default. Since API 24.0, tests see only data they create, plus setup objects like `User`, `Profile` and `RecordType`.

flashcards.front: What does `@TestSetup` do?
flashcards.back: It creates records once, before the test methods run. Each test method starts from those original records. Only one per class.

flashcards.front: How does `Test.loadData` get its records?
flashcards.back: From a CSV file saved as a static resource. The first line holds field names. It inserts the rows and returns them.

flashcards.front: Are records changed under `SeeAllData=true` saved?
flashcards.back: No. `SeeAllData=true` only lets the test read org data. Anything it inserts, updates or deletes is still rolled back.

flashcards.front: What do `Test.startTest()` and `Test.stopTest()` do?
flashcards.back: Code between them gets a fresh set of governor limits. Async calls made after `startTest` run synchronously at `stopTest`.

flashcards.front: How many times can a test method call `Test.startTest()`?
flashcards.back: Once. The same goes for `Test.stopTest()`.

flashcards.front: How many `execute` calls of a batch job can one test run?
flashcards.back: One. Keep test records within one batch scope, which is 200 by default.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between `Limits.getQueries()` and `Limits.getLimitQueries()`?
flashcards.back: `getQueries()` is how many SOQL queries are used so far. `getLimitQueries()` is the maximum allowed in this context.

flashcards.front: How does a test run a trigger?
flashcards.back: By doing DML on the trigger's object, like `insert` or `update`. Triggers can't be called by name.

flashcards.front: What does `System.runAs` do in a test?
flashcards.back: Runs a block as another user, with that user's record sharing. Object and field permissions count only where the code checks them. Works only in tests; avoids mixed DML errors.

flashcards.front: How do you test a Visualforce controller extension?
flashcards.back: Set the page with `Test.setCurrentPage`, build a `StandardController` around a test record and pass it to the extension's constructor.

flashcards.front: Why add `Assert.fail()` in a negative test?
flashcards.back: So the test fails if no exception is thrown. Put it right after the DML that should fail.

flashcards.front: What are the debug log levels, quiet to loud?
flashcards.back: `NONE`, `ERROR`, `WARN`, `INFO`, `DEBUG`, `FINE`, `FINER`, `FINEST`. Each level includes everything quieter.

flashcards.front: How long are debug logs kept?
flashcards.back: System debug logs: 24 hours. Monitoring logs: 7 days. Each log is at most 20 MB.

flashcards.front: Does a trace flag on a class create debug logs?
flashcards.back: No. Class and trigger trace flags change log levels, but logs come only when logging is on, like from a user trace flag.

flashcards.front: Which log category shows flow events?
flashcards.back: Workflow. It covers workflow rules, flows and processes.

flashcards.front: Are records inserted with Execute Anonymous saved?
flashcards.back: Yes, if the block finishes without errors. If it fails, all its changes roll back. It isn't a test.

flashcards.front: How do you query code coverage objects in the Developer Console?
flashcards.back: In the Query Editor, tick Use Tooling API. Then query `ApexCodeCoverageAggregate` or `ApexCodeCoverage`.

flashcards.front: What is a Developer Console checkpoint?
flashcards.back: A marker on a line of Apex. When the line runs, it captures the objects in memory, with no code change.

flashcards.front: Who does anonymous Apex run as?
flashcards.back: The current user. It can fail to compile if it breaks that user's object or field permissions.

flashcards.front: How long does a scratch org last?
flashcards.back: 1 to 30 days, 7 by default. Once it expires, it can't be restored.

flashcards.front: What do you need before creating scratch orgs?
flashcards.back: A Dev Hub org, a Salesforce DX project and a scratch org definition file, usually `config/project-scratch-def.json`.

flashcards.front: Which CLI commands move source in and out of an org?
flashcards.back: `sf project deploy start` sends local source to the org. `sf project retrieve start` pulls org changes into the project.

flashcards.front: Which CLI command shows debug logs live in the terminal?
flashcards.back: `sf apex tail log`. It turns on logging and prints logs as they arrive.

flashcards.front: What are the four sandbox types and their refresh intervals?
flashcards.back: Developer: 1 day. Developer Pro: 1 day. Partial Copy: 5 days. Full: 29 days.

flashcards.front: Which sandboxes copy data?
flashcards.back: Partial Copy copies a sample chosen by a template. Full copies all data. Developer and Developer Pro copy metadata only.

flashcards.front: Which sandbox needs a template?
flashcards.back: Partial Copy always needs one. A Full sandbox can use one, but it's optional.

flashcards.front: Which sandbox fits load and performance testing?
flashcards.back: Full. It copies all data and has the same storage as production.

flashcards.front: What are the four main deploy test levels?
flashcards.back: `NoTestRun` (dev orgs only), `RunSpecifiedTests` (75% per component), `RunLocalTests` (production default with Apex), `RunAllTestsInOrg` (packages too).

flashcards.front: Can a change set delete a component?
flashcards.back: No. Change sets only add or update. Delete with a destructive changes manifest through the Metadata API or Salesforce CLI.

flashcards.front: What is a quick deploy?
flashcards.back: Deploying a validation that passed in the last 10 days, without running tests again.

flashcards.front: How do you check on a batch or Queueable job?
flashcards.back: Use its job Id. Open Apex Jobs in Setup, or query `AsyncApexJob` for `Status`, `JobItemsProcessed`, `TotalJobItems` and `NumberOfErrors`.

questions.q: A developer is ready to move a new Apex class from a sandbox to production. What does Salesforce require of the org's Apex tests?
options: Tests cover at least 65% of the Apex code, and failures are allowed in classes outside the deployment
Tests cover 100% of triggers and at least 50% of classes
Each new class has its own test class with at least one assert in every method
Tests cover at least 75% of the Apex code, and all of those tests pass
questions.explain: Production needs at least 75% coverage, and all tests must pass. Every trigger also needs some coverage. Think: three-quarters, no red.
wrong: The bar is 75%, and failing tests block the deploy.
Triggers need some coverage, not 100%, and classes count toward the 75% total.
Asserts are best practice, but the gate counts coverage, not asserts per method.

questions.q: Which annotation tells Salesforce that a method is a unit test?

`@TestSetup`
`@IsTest`
`@Testable`
questions.explain: Test methods and test classes are marked with `@IsTest`. The old `testMethod` keyword does the same, but `@IsTest` is the recommended way.
wrong: `@TestVisible` lets tests see private members; it doesn't make a test.
`@TestSetup` marks a method that creates shared test data.
There is no `@Testable` annotation in Apex.

questions.q: A developer is reviewing why a class shows lower coverage than expected. Which two kinds of lines are left out of the code coverage calculation? (Choose 2)

Calls to `System.debug`
SOQL queries inside `for` loops
Lines inside classes annotated `@IsTest`
`return` statements in private methods
questions.explain: Only executable lines in non-test code are counted. `System.debug` calls and test classes are left out, as are comments and blank lines.
wrong: Lines that didn't run count as uncovered, which lowers the percentage.
A query in a loop is a normal executable line and is counted.
A `return` is executable, so it is counted whether or not the method is private.

questions.q: All tests pass, and the coverage report is shown below. A deployment to production that includes these components still fails the coverage check. Why?

...
Org Wide Coverage   91%

NAME                 PERCENT
OrderService         96%
InvoiceService       89%
ShipmentTrigger      0%
OrderTrigger         100%
options: `ShipmentTrigger` has no test coverage at all
Each trigger needs 90% coverage of its own
Production requires a separate test class for each trigger
`InvoiceService` is covered below the 91% org-wide number
questions.explain: Every trigger must have some coverage, even when the org total is high. `ShipmentTrigger` at 0% blocks the deploy.
wrong: There is no 90% rule for triggers; they need some coverage.
One test class can cover many triggers; no one-to-one rule exists.
Classes only need to keep the org total at 75% or more.

questions.q: A tech lead writes the team's testing checklist. Which two items match Salesforce's testing best practices? (Choose 2)
options: Turn on `SeeAllData=true` so tests use realistic org records
Assume record Ids are created in ascending order
Use the `Assert` class methods to prove the code behaves correctly
Put every scenario for the whole app into one large test method
Exercise bulk trigger logic with at least 20 records
questions.explain: Good tests prove behavior and handle bulk. Use `Assert` methods to check results, and use at least 20 records for trigger tests.
wrong: Tests should create their own data, not depend on org records.
Record Ids aren't guaranteed to be in order.
Test classes individually; never test the whole app in one test.

SELECT ApexClassOrTrigger.Name, NumLinesCovered, NumLinesUncovered
FROM ______
WHERE ApexClassOrTrigger.Name = 'TaskUtil'
options: `ApexTestResult`
`ApexCodeCoverage`
`AsyncApexJob`
`ApexCodeCoverageAggregate`
questions.explain: `ApexCodeCoverageAggregate` sums the coverage of every test method for a class. `ApexCodeCoverage` keeps one row per test method instead.
wrong: `ApexTestResult` holds pass or fail outcomes, not line counts.
`ApexCodeCoverage` stores coverage for each test method separately.
`AsyncApexJob` tracks async jobs, not coverage.

questions.q: A test class gives `ShippingCalc` 100% coverage, yet users report wrong shipping fees in production. What is the main weakness of this test?
options: `Test.startTest()` is missing, so the coverage isn't counted
It has no assert, so a wrong fee still passes
The class must be `public` for the framework to run it
It must insert records to record coverage
questions.explain: Coverage shows that lines ran, not that they were right. This test has no assert, so it passes whatever `fee` is. Add `Assert.areEqual` with the expected fee.
wrong: Coverage is recorded with or without `startTest`.
Test classes can be private; access level doesn't matter.
Coverage doesn't need records; any executed line counts.

questions.q: Before a release, the team checks coverage. The deployment runs with the default test level for production and includes Apex. Org-wide coverage is 81%. `RefundService` is at 60%, and every trigger has some coverage. All tests pass. What happens?
options: The deployment fails because `RefundService` is below 75%
The deployment fails because coverage must be 85% with new classes
The deployment succeeds because the org-wide total is above 75%
The deployment succeeds only if `RefundService` is listed in a test suite
questions.explain: The default production level, `RunLocalTests`, checks coverage across the org. At 81% overall, with every trigger covered and all tests passing, the deploy succeeds.
wrong: A per-class 75% check applies only to `RunSpecifiedTests`.
No 85% rule exists; 75% is the bar.
Test suites only group tests to run; they don't change the coverage rule.

questions.q: A developer adds a test method directly to the `InvoiceService` class, as shown. The class is saved at API 64.0. What happens?

It saves, and the method runs in every deployment test run
It saves, but its coverage counts against the code size limit
It fails to save, because test methods must sit in a test class
questions.explain: Since API 28.0, test methods can't live in non-test classes. Move the method into a separate class marked `@IsTest`.
wrong: The class doesn't save at all, so the method never runs.
Nothing runs: the class fails to compile.
The problem isn't the size limit; the class doesn't compile.

questions.q: A test method inserts 50 Contacts. What happens to those Contacts when the test finishes?
options: They stay in the org until a developer deletes them
They are rolled back and never saved
They move to the Recycle Bin for 15 days
They stay only if the test passes
questions.explain: Test data is never committed. Everything a test inserts or changes is rolled back when it ends, so you never need to delete it.
wrong: Tests don't commit data, so nothing is left behind.
Rolled-back records never existed, so nothing goes to the Recycle Bin.
Pass or fail, test data is always rolled back.

questions.q: A developer wants to create shared records once, before any test method in the class runs. Which annotation should they use?
options: `@TestVisible`
`@TestSetup`
`@IsTest(SeeAllData=true)`
`@IsTest(OnInstall=true)`
questions.explain: `@TestSetup` runs once before the test methods. Each test method then starts from those same records.
wrong: `@TestVisible` exposes private members to tests.
`SeeAllData=true` opens org data; it doesn't create anything.
`OnInstall=true` picks tests to run during package install.

questions.q: A sandbox has an Account named Acme and a profile named Standard User. A test class has no `SeeAllData` setting. Inside a test method, the developer queries both. What do the queries return?
questions.code:
Profile p = [SELECT Id FROM Profile WHERE Name = 'Standard User'];

options: Both records, since tests see the sandbox's data
Neither record, since tests see no existing data
The Standard User profile, but not the Acme Account
The Acme Account, but not the Standard User profile record
questions.explain: Tests can't see org data by default, but they can see setup objects. A `Profile` is a setup object; an Account is business data.
wrong: Since API 24.0, tests can't see existing business records.
Setup objects like `Profile` and `User` stay visible.
It's the other way around: Accounts are hidden, profiles are visible.

questions.code:
Code__c,Percent__c,Active__c
SPRING10,10,true

Paste the rows into a `@TestVisible` constant on the class
Use `@IsTest(SeeAllData=true)` and import the spreadsheet into the org
Upload the rows as a CSV static resource and call `Test.loadData`

Tests shouldn't depend on org data, and it ties the test to one org.

questions.q: A developer is adding a `@TestSetup` method to a test class. Which two statements about it are true? (Choose 2)
options: A class can have one `@TestSetup` method for each object it creates
It also works in a class marked `@IsTest(SeeAllData=true)`
It runs once, before any test method in the class
Changes one test method makes to its records are seen by later methods
Each test method sees its records in their original state
questions.explain: `@TestSetup` runs once before the test methods. Each method's changes roll back, so the next method sees the original records.
wrong: Only one test setup method is allowed per class.
Test setup isn't supported in a class with `SeeAllData=true`.
Changes roll back after each test method.

questions.q: This test reads an existing Account and inserts a new one named Acme Test. After the test run, where is Acme Test?
options: It is gone; the insert was rolled back
It stays in the org, since the test could see org data
It stays until the next test run
It is saved, but only visible to the running user
questions.explain: `SeeAllData=true` only opens read access to org data. New and changed records are still rolled back.
wrong: Seeing org data doesn't mean saving to it; changes still roll back.
Nothing is saved, so there is nothing to delete later.
Test data is never saved for anyone.

questions.q: A developer reviews this test class. What happens when `seesOnlyOwnData` runs?
options: It still sees all org data; the method setting is ignored
It sees only data it creates, since the method setting wins
The class fails to compile, since the two settings conflict
It sees org data only for objects it doesn't insert
questions.explain: When the class has `SeeAllData=true`, a method's `SeeAllData=false` is ignored. The method still sees all org data. The reverse override does work: method `true` beats class `false`.
wrong: A method can open data access but can't close it under a `true` class.
It compiles; the method's setting is simply ignored.
Data access isn't split by object like that.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using the isTest(SeeAllData=True) Annotation

questions.q: Both test methods below run in the same class. What is the result?
options: Both tests pass, since each method sees the original setup records
`checksStatus` fails, since `closes` already changed the Account
`checksStatus` fails, since setup records exist only for the first method
Both tests fail, since setup records can't be updated in a test
questions.explain: Each test method's changes roll back when it ends. So `checksStatus` sees `Active__c` as `true`, as `@TestSetup` made it, whatever order the methods run in.
wrong: The update in `closes` rolls back before the next method runs.
Setup records are available to every test method in the class.
Test methods can update setup records; the change just rolls back.

questions.q: A team moves its record-building helper methods from a regular `public` class into a `public` class marked `@IsTest`. Which two results follow? (Choose 2)
options: The helpers now run in production code paths faster
The class no longer counts toward the org's Apex code size limit
Lines inside the helpers now count toward code coverage
Only test code can call the helpers from now on
The helpers now commit their records so other tests can reuse them
questions.explain: A `@IsTest` utility class is excluded from the code size limit and runs only in test context. Non-test code can't call it.
wrong: Non-test code can't call an `@IsTest` class at all.
Test classes are left out of the coverage calculation.
Test data is never committed, wherever it's created.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Common Test Utility Classes for Test Data Creation

questions.q: How many times can a single test method call `Test.startTest()`?
options: Once per test class
Once per test method
Once per DML statement
As many times as needed
questions.explain: Each test method may call `startTest` once and `stopTest` once. The pair marks the one block that gets fresh limits.
wrong: The rule is per test method, not per class.
DML statements have nothing to do with this rule.
A second call isn't allowed in the same test method.

questions.q: This test fails on the assert, even though `ScoreJob` sets `Rating` to Hot correctly. What should the developer change?
options: Wrap `System.enqueueJob` in a `try` block
Call `Test.startTest()` a second time before the assert
Move the query and assert after `Test.stopTest()`
Switch `ScoreJob` to a `@future` method
questions.explain: Async work queued after `startTest` runs when `stopTest` is called. Here the assert runs first, so the job hasn't run yet. Assert after `stopTest`.
wrong: The job didn't fail; it just hasn't run yet.
`startTest` can only be called once per test method.
A future method has the same timing; it also runs at `stopTest`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Limits, startTest, and stopTest

questions.q: A test method runs 98 SOQL queries during setup, then calls `Test.startTest()`. Between `startTest` and `stopTest`, the code runs 40 queries. After `Test.stopTest()`, how many more queries can the test run before it hits the synchronous limit of 100?
options: None
60 more
100 more
2 more
questions.explain: `startTest` adds a fresh context; it doesn't reset the original one. After `stopTest`, the test is back in the first context, which already used 98 of 100.
wrong: The 40 queries were counted in the separate block, not the original context.
The block's 60 unused queries don't carry over after `stopTest`.
The original context isn't reset; it still holds the 98 setup queries.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Limits, startTest, and stopTest

questions.q: What two things happen when a test calls `Test.stopTest()`? (Choose 2)
options: All test data created so far is committed to the database
Async calls made after `startTest` run synchronously
Static variables reset to their starting values
The test goes back to the limits it had before the block began
Records inserted between `startTest` and `stopTest` are deleted
questions.explain: `stopTest` runs the collected async work right away. Then code after it uses the original limits from before `startTest`.
wrong: Test data is never committed.
`stopTest` doesn't touch static variables.
Records stay until the whole test method ends, then roll back.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Limits, startTest, and stopTest

questions.q: A developer wants to log how many SOQL queries the code under test has already used. Which call returns that number?
options: `Limits.getQueries()`
`Limits.getLimitQueries()`
`Test.getQueries()`
`System.getQueryCount()`
questions.explain: Each `Limits` method has two forms. `getQueries()` returns what's used so far; `getLimitQueries()` returns the maximum.
wrong: `getLimitQueries()` returns the maximum allowed, not the count used.
The `Test` class has no `getQueries` method.
There is no `System.getQueryCount` method.

options: `stopTest` runs only the `start` method, so nothing is processed
The 500 inserts exceed the DML row limit for a test
Batch jobs can't be started from a test method
Only one `execute` call can run in a test; this needs three
questions.explain: A test can test only one run of `execute`. With the default size of 200, 500 records need three runs. Insert 200 or fewer, or pass a larger scope.
wrong: `stopTest` runs the whole job: `start`, `execute` and `finish`.
500 rows is far below the 10,000 DML row limit.
Tests can start batch jobs; put `executeBatch` inside the start-stop block.

questions.q: A developer wrote this test without `Test.startTest()` and `Test.stopTest()`. `CloseStaleCases` closes every Case it finds. Why does the assert fail?
options: The batch runs when the test method ends, after the assert
Batch jobs never run in tests unless the class is `public`
Without `startTest`, the batch job is discarded and never runs
The query runs before the insert of the Case is committed
questions.explain: An `executeBatch` outside the start-stop block runs when the test method ends. The assert runs first and sees the Case still open. Wrap the call in `startTest` and `stopTest`.
wrong: Access level doesn't control whether a batch runs in a test.
The job isn't discarded; it runs at the end of the method.
The insert is visible to the query in the same test; tests just never commit.

questions.q: In this test method, where should the developer insert the test records that `ReminderService` needs?
options: At B, inside the start-stop block
At C, after `Test.stopTest()` and before the assert
In a separate class marked `@IsTest(SeeAllData=true)`
At A, before `Test.startTest()` is called
questions.explain: Create all test data before calling `startTest`. Then the fresh limits measure only the code you're testing, and the data exists when `sendDue` runs.
wrong: Setup inside the block uses up limits meant for the code under test.
The code under test needs the data before it runs.
`SeeAllData=true` reads org data; it doesn't help you build test data.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Testing Best Practices

questions.q: A batch class throws an unhandled exception inside `execute` during a test. Which two statements describe what happens? (Choose 2)

The exception is logged and the test passes
To handle it, the `catch` block must come after `Test.stopTest()`
The batch retries the chunk once before failing
The test fails only if `finish` also throws an exception
questions.explain: In a test, exceptions from a batch job pass to the calling test method, so it fails. To handle one, wrap the code in `try` and put the `catch` after `stopTest`, where the job runs.
wrong: The exception reaches the test method, so it fails.
Batch jobs don't retry a failed chunk.
An exception in `execute` is enough to fail the test.

Insert Opportunity records so the trigger fires
Run the trigger from Execute Anonymous
Mark the trigger with `@IsTest`

Anonymous Apex isn't a test and gives no coverage for deployment.
`@IsTest` can't be put on a trigger.

`OrderSummaryExt ext = new OrderSummaryExt(new ApexPages.StandardSetController(new List<Order>{ ord }));`

Insert a `PageReference` record with the `orderId` field filled in
Call `Test.startTest()`, which loads the page's URL parameters
Set `System.currentPageReference` to a new `Map` of parameters
questions.explain: `Test.setCurrentPage` sets the page a controller sees. Then `ApexPages.currentPage().getParameters().put('orderId', id)` adds the parameter before the constructor reads it.

questions.q: A developer is writing tests for a trigger that assigns Cases to queues. Which two approaches follow Salesforce best practice? (Choose 2)

Use `SeeAllData=true` so the test can use real queues and Cases

Test both valid Cases and Cases that should be rejected

Query the saved records and assert on their field values.

The assert inside `catch` always compares two equal values

options: The transaction fails with a debug log size limit error
The log is split into two separate logs
Logging stops, and later lines are lost
Older log lines are removed to bring it under 20 MB
